1.pericope_label: The elder unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth; and not I only, but also all they that have known the truth; For the truth’s sake, which dwelleth in us, and shall be with us for ever. Grace be with you, mercy, and peace, from God the Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love.

schools.summary: Gill takes up the two questions of identity. On the writer he offers alternatives without choosing: ‘the elder’ may be used on account of John’s age, since he was now near a hundred years old and had outlived all the apostles, or on account of his office as overseer not only of the church at Ephesus but of all the Asiatic churches — which he holds is the same thing as an elder and not incompatible with the apostolate. On the recipient he argues that the elect lady is an individual and not a church, both because a church is not usually spoken of in this way and because the writer plans to come and see her face to face. On the ground of the love he denies it lies in her high birth, nobility or riches, and gives three possible senses of ‘the truth’: Christ himself, who is the truth and dwells in believers by faith and is the same in one as in another; the Gospel, which has a place in every saint and is the same for matter and substance in all, so that unity of judgment produces unity of affection; or the truth of grace as an inward principle.

Henry reads the opening as a piece of consecrated convention. Ancient letters began, as this one does, with salutation and good wishes, and religion consecrates such old forms so far as it may, turning compliments into real expressions of life and love. He notes that the saluter is identified not by name but by a chosen character, and that the style and love of the letter suggest the same hand as the preceding epistle; the writer is now the elder emphatically and eminently, possibly the oldest apostle then living and the chief elder in the church of God. He then presses the dignity of the title: an elder in the ancient house of Israel was to be reverenced, and much more one in the gospel Israel of God, an old disciple being honourable and an old apostle and leader of disciples more so.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson divide the introduction, the situation and the grammar. Barnes gives an extended account of the canonical question, reporting that the authenticity of the second and third epistles was doubted by many in the early church and that their canonical authority was not fully admitted for a considerable time, while the first was always received as undoubtedly John’s; he attributes the doubt to their exceeding brevity and to their being addressed to individuals and apparently not designed for general circulation, which made the early writers cite them less and makes their genuineness harder to establish. On the second verse he explains the love as love of the truth exemplified in this family, truth having taken a permanent abode in every heart that loves religion; on the third he observes that the salutation differs from the usual apostolic form only in its emphasis on the Lord Jesus as the Son of the Father, which is much in John’s manner. Ellicott reconstructs the situation from the address: a man so well known to his correspondent that he calls himself only ‘the old man’ writes to a mother, whose name is possibly Kyria, and to her children, while her sister’s children are in the same place as the writer, and both mothers are honoured with the religious title ‘elect’. Robertson notes that the children may be understood literally or spiritually; that the relative pronoun is masculine plural where the noun is neuter, a construction according to sense which embraces the mother and the children of both sexes; that the closing clause of the second verse is a confident assertion and not a wish, the future indicative standing where other epistles have an optative; that the third verse picks up the same words in reverse order; that the salutation resembles those of the Pastoral Epistles, grace being the wellspring in the heart of God, mercy its outpourings and peace its blessed effect; and that the repetition of the preposition before Jesus Christ is unique, serving to bring out distinctly the twofold personal relation of man to the Father and to the Son.

Clarke and Wesley take opposite halves of the passage. Clarke argues for authenticity from style: the authority of the First Epistle being established, little needs saying of the second and third, since their language and sentiment so fully accord with it that whoever wrote one wrote all three. He does not conceal the counter-evidence, that doubts were entertained in the primitive Church and that as late as the fourth century these were still ranked among the writings not received by all, and he suggests that being letters to private persons they simply circulated less. On the second verse he takes the truth as the Gospel and the promise as one of preservation, God keeping not only the Christian religion but all its essential doctrines for ever, and he records a strange Armenian reading here which no other version or manuscript supports. On the third he holds that the phrase ‘the Son of the Father’ keeps the miraculous conception in view, a doctrine the Gnostics absolutely denied and one that lies at the groundwork of salvation. Wesley calls ‘the elder’ an appellation suited to a familiar letter upon a weighty subject, glosses ‘elect’ simply as Christian, and insists that Kyria is undoubtedly a proper name both here and later in the letter, since the title of lady was not then given to any but the Roman empress and such a manner of speaking would not suit the simplicity and dignity of the apostle. On the salutation he distinguishes the three terms — grace takes away guilt, mercy misery, and peace implies abiding in grace and mercy — calling it the very foretaste of heaven, and treats faith and truth as synonymous in the closing phrase.

debates: Whether the letter is genuinely John’s. Barnes sets out the early doubts at length and explains them by the letter’s brevity and private address; Clarke argues from the identity of language and sentiment with the First Epistle that one hand wrote all three, while granting that as late as the fourth century they were still counted among the disputed books.

Who the elect lady is. Gill argues she is an individual rather than a church, since a church is not usually so described and since the writer intends to visit her; Wesley holds Kyria is a proper name outright, on the ground that ‘lady’ was then reserved to the Roman empress; Ellicott allows the name only as a possibility.

Whether the children are natural or spiritual. Robertson leaves both open, noting that the word bears either sense elsewhere in the New Testament, and observes that the relative pronoun follows the sense rather than the grammatical gender so as to take in mother and children together.

What ‘the truth’ denotes in the second verse. Gill offers three senses — Christ, the Gospel, and the inward principle of grace — without deciding; Barnes takes it as the gospel embraced and permanently lodged in the heart; Clarke reads it as the body of essential doctrine that God will preserve for ever; Wesley as a living principle of faith and holiness.
outliers: Clarke alone reads a doctrinal polemic into the salutation, taking ‘the Son of the Father’ as an assertion of the miraculous conception against the Gnostics, where Barnes finds in the same words only a characteristic emphasis of John’s.
Henry alone comments on the epistolary convention itself, treating the borrowed form of ancient letters as something religion consecrates rather than as a neutral frame.
themes: the elect lady and her children
truth dwelling in us for ever

4.pericope_label: I rejoiced greatly that I found of thy children walking in truth, as we have received a commandment from the Father. And now I beseech thee, lady, not as though I wrote a new commandment unto thee, but that which we had from the beginning, that we love one another. And this is love, that we walk after his commandments. This is the commandment, That, as ye have heard from the beginning, ye should walk in it.

schools.summary: Gill reads the partitive expression strictly and draws a doctrine from it: the apostle found some of her children walking in truth, not all, since good parents have not always good children, or at least not all of them — Adam had a Cain, Abraham an Ishmael, Isaac an Esau — and God is pleased to show his discriminating grace in tribes and families by taking some and leaving others, so that it is a great mercy when instead of the fathers are the children. On the address he notes that the Syriac and Arabic versions keep the word Kyria as though it were a proper name. On the definition of love he takes the walking after God’s commandments as observing them for a rule of conversation, by which love is shown to God, and adds that such may expect fresh discoveries of the love of God to them in return.

Henry attends to the tone of the request and to the family. On the children he makes the verse an encouragement: it is good to be trained to early religion, children may be beloved for their parents’ sake, and it gave the apostle great joy to see children treading in their parents’ steps and likely in their turn to support the gospel — which he contrasts with the many who spread irreligion, infidelity and vice among their own children. On the request he finds the manner of address very remarkable, since what is asked is not any particular boon or bounty to the writer but common duty and the observance of a divine command, so that he might have commanded or charged outright; but harsher measures are worse than needless where milder will prevail, and the apostolical spirit is of all others the most tender and endearing, so that whether out of deference to her ladyship or out of apostolical meekness, or both, he condescends to beseech. He also grants that the commandment of mutual Christian love may be called new in respect of its being declared by the Lord Christ, while as to the matter it is old.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson supply the circumstances and the grammar. Barnes notes that the apostle does not say how he learned the fact and that the verb would suit either personal acquaintance or report, records Grotius’s conjecture that some of the sons had come to Ephesus on business and were met there, and observes that the wording implies he knew of a part of the family only; on the address he thinks the familiar style unobjectionable if Cyria was her name, John being then probably very old and the woman much younger; on the commandment he holds that John presumed it understood as far as the gospel was known, and might well presume it, since Christianity never prevails anywhere without prompting obedience to this law; and he calls the walking after the commandments the proper evidence of love and the peculiar commandment by which the disciples are to be distinguished in the world. Ellicott takes the children as probably those met at home, and gives the fullest analysis of the love in question: it is the Christian’s moral disposition of mind, embracing all other virtues and graces — implying faith, because founded on Christian principle and testable only by a right belief; purity, because modelled on the love of God and having abjured the old man; and unselfishness, because it desires the good of the other. Robertson finds a glad surprise in the aorist, notes that the adverb for ‘greatly’ occurs only here and in the third epistle among John’s writings, treats the perfect as our own ‘eureka’ marking a continued discovery, and quotes the picture of the writer sitting down at once to write to Kyria, glad that her lads far away in the great city were true to their early faith; he observes that the plural ‘we had’ is not literary but identifies all Christians with the writer, and leaves undecided whether the closing ‘in it’ refers to the truth, the love or the commandment, thinking love the likeliest.

Clarke and Wesley reconstruct the household and date the commandment. Clarke supposes the matron to be the mother of a family and probably a widow, since no husband is mentioned, and also a deaconess of the church in whose house the travelling evangelists preached and were entertained; on that reading the children may be her own, or members of the church under her care, or some of both, and the apostle learned the news either from a letter of her own or from the itinerant evangelists. He dates the commandment from the first publication of Christianity, states that love is the principle of obedience, and takes the mode of address as showing that a person and not a church is written to. Wesley supposes the children were found in their aunt’s house, on the strength of the letter’s closing verse; dates the commandment from the beginning of our Lord’s ministry while allowing that in some sense it was from the beginning of the world; and calls universal obedience built on the love of God the proof of true love.

debates: Where the children were met. Barnes reports Grotius’s conjecture of a business visit to Ephesus and declines to decide; Wesley infers their aunt’s house from the closing verse; Ellicott supposes they were at home; Robertson quotes a reconstruction that places them far away in the great city. The text supports none of these directly, and each witness says so in his own way.

How much of the family is meant. Gill presses the partitive strictly and builds on it a doctrine of discriminating grace; Barnes draws the same limitation from the wording without the doctrine; Henry passes over the limitation and treats the verse as encouragement to household religion.

In what sense the commandment is not new. Clarke dates it from the first publication of Christianity; Wesley from our Lord’s ministry, and in some sense from the beginning of the world; Henry distinguishes the declaration by Christ, which is new, from the matter, which is old.

Who the recipient is. Clarke argues from the mode of address that a person is written to rather than a church; Gill notes that the Syriac and Arabic treat the word as a name; Barnes accepts the name as a working assumption and explains the familiarity by the difference in age.
outliers: Henry alone makes the courtesy of the request the subject of comment, observing that the apostle could have commanded and chose to beseech, and treating that choice as characteristic of the apostolic spirit rather than as deference to rank alone.
Ellicott alone analyses love into its implied components — faith, purity and unselfishness — where the other witnesses define it by its effect, as obedience to the commandments.
themes: some but not all of a household
the elect lady addressed by name
the apostle beseeching rather than charging

7.pericope_label: For many deceivers are entered into the world, who confess not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh. This is a deceiver and an antichrist. Look to yourselves, that we lose not those things which we have wrought, but that we receive a full reward. Whosoever transgresseth, and abideth not in the doctrine of Christ, hath not God. He that abideth in the doctrine of Christ, he hath both the Father and the Son.

schools.summary: Gill describes the deceivers by quality and by number: they are deceitful workers who pretend to be ministers of Christ, to have a value for truth, a love for souls and a view to the glory of God, while they lie in wait to deceive and handle the word of God deceitfully; and they are many, and so likely to do much mischief. He records that the Alexandrian copy and some others, with the Vulgate and Syriac versions, read that they are gone out into the world rather than entered into it. The exhortation he takes simply, as a charge to the lady and her children to look about them, take care of themselves and beware of these men and their doctrines. On the last verse he is careful about the word: the transgression meant is not of the law of God, of which everyone is a transgressor daily in thought, word or deed, but of the rule and standard of doctrine, which such a man will not adhere to or walk by, but rejects and despises.

Henry treats the verse as news delivered for a purpose. He calls it the ill news communicated to the lady, that seducers are abroad, and observes that the report is introduced by a particle which bespeaks a reason for it: she has need to maintain her love, because there are destroyers of it in the world, and those who subvert the faith destroy the love, since the common faith is one ground of the common love; or else the reason attaches to the walking just commanded, her stability being likely to be tried. He draws from this a rule about communication itself: sad and saddening news may properly be told to our Christian friends, not that we should love to make them sorry, but in order to forewarn them.

Barnes and Robertson divide the passage between argument and text. Barnes detaches the opening conjunction from the preceding verse, holding that it introduces the caution which follows rather than a reason for mutual love, so that the sense is: since many deceivers are abroad, look to yourselves. On the exhortation he gives a rule of priority — the first care must be to secure one’s own heart, since when error abounds our first duty is not to attack it and make war upon it but to look to the citadel of our own souls and see it well guarded, as an invaded country does not send men out against the enemy regardless of its own strength or the security of its fortresses. On the last verse he finds the phrase ‘the doctrine of Christ’ as ambiguous as ‘the love of Christ’, declines to settle whether it means the doctrine Christ taught or the true doctrine concerning him, reports Macknight’s view that it is what Christ and his apostles taught, and inclines to that while noting it would include all Christ said of himself. Robertson notes that the word for deceiver means wandering or roving and is used in the New Testament of Jesus by his enemies and of Paul; treats the reading ‘are gone forth’ as correct and hears in it an allusion to the moment when these men left the churches; settles the disputed clause on the manuscripts, making the two verbs second person while the intervening clause about what was wrought remains first, since John does not wish his own labour lost; and decides that the doctrine of Christ is the teaching of Christ and not teaching about him, the standard of Christian teaching as his walk is the standard of the Christian’s walk. He also explains the force of the word rendered ‘transgresseth’: it means going on ahead, which is often the very thing to do, and takes its bad sense only from the clause beside it — the Gnostics being the self-styled progressives and advanced thinkers, anxious to relegate Christ to the past in their onward march.

Clarke and Wesley identify the error and weigh the disputed reading. Clarke names the deceivers as Gnostics, since they denied that Jesus was come in the flesh, and observes that a doctrine so essential to salvation could be denied by none but a deceiver and an antichrist; he notes that many excellent manuscripts and versions read ‘are gone out’ for ‘are entered in’, with nearly the same sense, and that many manuscripts, versions and fathers put the whole clause about losing and receiving in the second person, a reading he judges more consistent and likely, though he also explains the received text by having the apostles fear to be deprived of their converts as their crown of rejoicing. On the last verse he takes the verb as passing over a sacred enclosure and going beyond the prescribed limits, and promises the one who abides within them communion with the Father as Father and with the Son as Saviour. Wesley reads the denial more broadly, of any who disbelieve Christ’s prophetic, priestly or kingly office; keeps the first person in the disputed clause and explains it as modesty, the apostle transferring to himself what belongs to them, adding that to lose what has been wrought is exactly what every apostate does; and refers the transgression to any law of God rather than to a rule of doctrine.

debates: Whether the deceivers entered the world or went out of it. Gill and Clarke both record the variant without deciding, Clarke judging the sense nearly the same; Robertson takes the going out as the true reading and finds in it an allusion to the moment these men left the churches.

Whether the eighth verse is first person or second. Clarke reports strong support for ‘ye lose’ and ‘ye receive’ and prefers it; Robertson makes the same division but keeps ‘which we have wrought’ in the first person; Wesley retains the first person throughout and reads it as apostolic modesty.

What ‘the doctrine of Christ’ means. Barnes calls the genitive ambiguous and will not settle it, though he inclines with Macknight to the teaching of Christ and his apostles; Robertson decides it outright as the teaching of Christ rather than teaching about him.

What is transgressed. Gill restricts it to the rule and standard of doctrine, expressly excluding the law of God since all transgress that daily; Clarke takes it as passing beyond a sacred enclosure; Wesley refers it plainly to any law of God.
How the opening conjunction connects. Barnes attaches it to the warning that follows; Henry attaches it to the request that precedes, making the deceivers a reason for maintaining love.
outliers: Barnes alone turns the exhortation into a general rule about the order of Christian duty, arguing that self-defence must precede any attack on error, and illustrating it from the defence of an invaded country.

Robertson alone reads the polemic historically, identifying the transgressors as men who called themselves progressive and sought to leave Christ behind, and finding that claim in the very verb the Authorised Version renders ‘transgresseth’.
themes: denying that Jesus is come in the flesh
having both the Father and the Son

10.pericope_label: If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed: For he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds.

schools.summary: Gill keeps to definition. The person contemplated comes under the character of a preacher, so the refusal is not of ordinary hospitality; and to bid such a man God speed is to wish him well and success in his ministry, or else to converse with him in a friendly and familiar way.

Henry sets the direction against the household’s known habits. This lady was possibly like Gaius in the following epistle, a generous housekeeper and a hospitable entertainer of travelling ministers and Christians, so that these deceivers might well expect the reception given to others, or to the best who came there. The apostle’s direction is accordingly negative — support them not — and rests on a principle: they are not to be entertained as ministers of Christ, because the Lord Christ will distinguish them from such and would have his disciples distinguish them too.

Barnes and Robertson both fix the scope of the prohibition and refuse to let it become general. Barnes takes the comer as any professed teacher of religion, holds there can be no doubt this household was accustomed to entertain such men, and states the limit explicitly: the words cannot mean that no acts of kindness were to be shown in any circumstances, but that nothing was to be done which could fairly be construed as encouraging or countenancing them as religious teachers, so that in meeting them as neighbours or strangers we are still to be honest, true and kind. To bid such a man God speed, he adds, shows that one countenances and approves the doctrine taught. Robertson insists that John is not referring to the entertainment of strangers at all but to deceiving propagandists who carried dissension and danger with them, notes that the house stands definite without the article like our own ‘at home’, and supplies the institutional fact behind the rule: the churches often met in private houses, so that if these travellers were allowed to spread their doctrine there and were then sent on with an endorsement, as Apollos was sent from Ephesus to Corinth, there was no escaping responsibility for the harm they did.

Clarke and Wesley both press the practical application, Clarke at length. He takes the comer as arriving under the character of an apostle or evangelist to preach in the house, so that refusing him means giving him no entertainment as an evangelical teacher and not letting him preach under that roof; he explains the greeting from eastern usage, since the words mean do not say Health to him or salute him with Peace be to thee, a salutation used among those of the same religion but not to strangers; and he gives the reason for withholding it, that to treat such a man as a sound Christian brother puts it in his power to deceive others by apparently accrediting his ministry. From this he draws a hard rule — that no sound Christian should countenance as a gospel minister any man who preaches erroneous doctrine, and that no Christian can attend such a ministry without being criminal in the sight of God, whether the teacher belongs to an established Church or to a congregation of dissenters — and then sets an express limit to it, that the apostle does not mean we should deny such men the common offices of humanity, charity and mercy. Wesley draws the line more widely than the others, refusing the man reception either as a teacher or as a brother, and holds that whoever gives him any encouragement is accessory to his evil deeds.

debates: How far the refusal extends. Barnes and Clarke both insist it is confined to countenancing the man as a religious teacher and does not touch ordinary kindness, charity or the common offices of humanity; Robertson reaches the same conclusion by denying that hospitality to strangers is in view at all; Wesley alone widens it, refusing reception as a brother as well as as a teacher.

What makes the greeting culpable. Gill defines it as wishing success to the ministry; Barnes as approving the doctrine; Clarke as accrediting the ministry to others; Wesley as giving encouragement; Robertson as furnishing the endorsement that carried a teacher on to the next house-church.

Why a private house should matter at all. Robertson answers from the practice of the churches, which met in private homes, so that admitting a teacher there was admitting him to a pulpit; Clarke reaches the same point by speaking of letting a man preach under one’s roof.
outliers: Clarke alone turns the verse into a rule about attending a ministry rather than admitting a teacher, and extends it explicitly across establishment and dissent, which none of the other witnesses does.
Henry alone reads the direction against the recipient’s reputation for hospitality, treating the warning as necessary precisely because her house was known to be open.
themes: receive him not into your house

12.pericope_label: Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full. The children of thy elect sister greet thee. Amen.

schools.summary: Gill turns both verses to controversy and to identification. On the unwritten remainder he suggests it may have concerned the state of the churches of Asia and particularly Ephesus, or private families and persons, or the doctrines of the gospel — but he denies it can have been any new doctrine, since the apostle has just disclaimed having any beyond what they heard from the beginning, and he concludes that the verse therefore makes nothing for the unwritten traditions of the Papists, as if the Scriptures did not contain the whole of doctrine and of the will of God. On the final greeting he denies that the elect sister denotes a sister church, as some think, and takes her for a sister according to the flesh, herself chosen of God to eternal life, whose children were walking in the truth and now send their Christian salutation to their aunt; he judges it very likely that these children lived at Ephesus, where John resided.

Henry treats the postponement as itself instructive. He calls it an adjournment of many things to personal conference, on the supposition that some things are better spoken than written: the use of pen and ink may be a mercy and a pleasure, but a personal interview may be more so. From the promise of a visit he infers that the apostle was not yet too old for travel, and therefore not too old for travelling service; and he draws the general rule that the communion of saints should be maintained by all methods and should tend to their mutual joy, excellent ministers having their own joy advanced by their Christian friends.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson attend to the circumstances and to the materials. Barnes reads the sentence as the language of one hurried, or in feeble health, or hoping soon to meet the person written to, so that only the points of most immediate and pressing importance are selected and the rest reserved for a free personal interview; he warns that the English word ‘paper’ conveys an idea which is not strictly correct, since paper as now understood was invented long afterwards and the material meant was the Egyptian papyrus; and on the last verse he observes that nothing more is known of the elect sister, inferring from her not being mentioned as sending a greeting of her own that she was probably dead or absent, while noting that John still names her as one of the chosen of God. Ellicott takes the verse as showing that this letter was not a mere accompaniment to a copy of the First Epistle, and describes the materials in detail: the ink a mixture of soot, water and gum; the papyrus growing in the swamps of the Nile to ten feet and more, the paper prepared from the thin coats surrounding the plant, the pieces joined by the turbid Nile water for its glutinous property, one layer laid flat on a board and a cross layer set over it. Robertson notes the epistolary aorist, describes the papyrus leaf as prepared by cutting the pith into strips and pasting them together, observes that the word for ink is the old adjective for black, remarks that John apparently wrote this little letter with his own hand, and gives the closing phrase its literal sense of mouth to mouth.

Clarke and Wesley both keep to the reason for brevity. Clarke has the apostle say in effect that he has many things he might write but thinks it best not to commit them to paper, since he hopes to visit shortly and speak fully, which will increase the comfort of the household and his own; and he states the principle behind it, that there is more comfort in mutual interviews among friends than in epistolary correspondence. Wesley reduces the matter to a sentence, that having many things to write the apostle was not minded to write now, and confined himself to what was then peculiarly needful.

debates: What the unwritten remainder would have contained. Gill canvasses the state of the Asian churches, private persons, and the doctrines of the gospel, while expressly excluding any new doctrine and turning the exclusion against the appeal to unwritten tradition; Barnes explains the brevity by the writer’s circumstances rather than by his subject; Wesley by the sufficiency of what was needful at the time.

Who the elect sister is. Gill denies she is a sister church and makes her a natural sister, chosen of God, whose children he supposes lived at Ephesus; Barnes admits nothing further is known, and infers from her silence in the greeting that she was dead or absent.
What the letter was for. Ellicott argues from the promise of a visit that this was an independent letter and not merely a covering note sent with a copy of the First Epistle.
outliers: Gill alone makes a doctrinal argument out of the apostle’s brevity, using the withheld remainder as evidence for the sufficiency of Scripture against unwritten tradition.

Ellicott alone treats the writing materials as a subject in their own right, describing the growth of the papyrus and the manufacture of the sheets at length where the others note only that the English word misleads.
themes: the elect sister and her children
